segments.text: Two everyday verbs — and together they make the Telugu goodbye.
వె (ve) + ళ్ళు (ḷḷu, a doubled retroflex ళ ḷ) becomes వెళ్ళు (veḷḷu). Its partner: వచ్చు (vaccu, "come") with the doubled చ్చ (cc).

వెళ్ళు (veḷḷu, "to go") and వచ్చు (vaccu, "to come") are native Dravidian verbs. As commands they are whole words: veḷḷu! ("go!"), rā! ("come!"). You need both, because Telugu — like every Dravidian language — does not say a plain "goodbye." It says "I go, and I come back."

lessons.title: వెళ్ళి వస్తాను (veḷḷi vastānu) — "I'll go and come back"

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The everyday Telugu goodbye — a promise, not a parting.
వెళ్ళి (veḷḷi, "having gone") is veḷḷu + the "-i" that means "having …d." వస్తాను (vastānu, "I come/will come") is from vaccu ("come") + "I."

వెళ్ళి వస్తాను (veḷḷi vastānu) = వెళ్ళి (veḷḷi, "having gone") + వస్తాను (vastānu, "I come") — literally "having gone, I come [back]," i.e. "I'll go and come back." A Telugu speaker never signs off with a bare "I'm leaving" — that sounds final. Instead they promise return. It is the same "go-and-come-back" farewell you meet across the Dravidian south (Tamil pōy varugiṟēṉ, Kannada hōgi baruttēne, Malayalam pōyi varāṁ) and echoing into the Indo-Aryan tracks (Bengali āshi). The warm reply is వెళ్ళి రండి (veḷḷi raṇḍi, "go and come [back]").

blocks.title: Across the family — the same idea, five ways

utterances: Language: Telugu. "go and come back" (goodbye): veḷḷi vastānu.
Language: Tamil. "go and come back" (goodbye): pōy varugiṟēṉ.
Language: Kannada. "go and come back" (goodbye): hōgi baruttēne.
Language: Malayalam. "go and come back" (goodbye): pōyi varāṁ.
Language: Bengali (Indo-Aryan). "go and come back" (goodbye): āshi ("I come").

segments.text: The whole south — and, in Bengali, well beyond it — prefers a promise of return to a blunt farewell. The languages are not all related; the habit travelled anyway.
Veḷḷi is Telugu's way of chaining actions: "having gone, (then) I come." Like its sisters, Telugu strings verbs with one in the participle form and the last one fully conjugated.

segments.text: A goodbye with a date on it.
రే (rē) + పు (pu) becomes రేపు (rēpu). కలుద్దాం (kaluddām) = kalu ("meet") + -ddām ("let's").

రేపు (rēpu, "tomorrow") is native Dravidian. కలుద్దాం (kaluddām, "let's meet") is from కలు (kalu, "to meet, to join") — so the phrase is "tomorrow, let's meet," the Telugu "see you tomorrow." The -దాం (-ddām) ending is Telugu's "let's ___" — a first-person-plural invitation: veḷḷddām ("let's go"), tindām ("let's eat").
రే (rē) + పు (pu) becomes రేపు. కలుద్దాం (kaludḍām) = kalu (“meet”) + -dḍām (“let's”).

segments.text: The open-ended, warm goodbye — no date, just a promise.
మళ్ళీ (maḷḷī): note the doubled retroflex ళ్ళ (ḷḷ), the same sound as in veḷḷu. కలుద్దాం (kaluddām, "let's meet") you just learned.

మళ్ళీ కలుద్దాం (maḷḷī kaluddām) = మళ్ళీ (maḷḷī, "again") + కలుద్దాం (kaluddām, "let's meet") — "we'll meet again." Both words are native Dravidian: maḷḷī ("again," from maral, "to return") and kalu ("to meet"). Where Tamil's "we'll meet again" (mīṇḍum sandippōm) reaches for the Sanskrit loan sandi to say "meet," Telugu keeps the native kalu — a small reminder that these sisters make the same phrase from different stock.
